articles.headline: Turbocharged Earnings Are Pushing Stocks Higher. There's a Catch
articles.text:
The stock market is salivating over big increases in corporate earnings, but there’s a catch. Much of the growth is due to a lag in when the costs of huge AI investments hit the books.
Analysts expect S&P 500 companies’ earnings growth to top 20% for a second consecutive quarter in the current period, in part because of soaring profits by semiconductor makers and other AI-infrastructure companies. This has lent crucial support to the booming stock market, helping keep valuation ratios in check.

articles.headline: Oracle Stock's High Stakes Gamble
articles.text:
If you hold Oracle (ORCL) stock, you've felt the turbulence. Despite a recent bounce, the shares are down over the last 12 months and sit well below their peak, a sign the market is wrestling with a profound shift in the company's story. The options market is pricing in elevated uncertainty, with implied volatility in the 67th percentile of its annual range. This isn't about a legacy business in decline; it's about the significant risks of a company going all-in on a new one.
Oracle is undertaking a large-scale, massive strategic pivot from a software titan into a capital-intensive AI infrastructure provider. The potential is considerable, but so is the price tag, and the biggest risks for investors are all tied to the sheer scale of this investment strategy.
The AI Bill Arrives
First, consider the raw financial commitment. To meet the surging demand for AI, management is planning for a "net cash outlay for capital expenditures of around $70 billion" in fiscal 2027. To fund this, the company expects to "raise around $40 billion in debt and equity." These are large figures that fundamentally alter the company's financial profile. The mechanism here is direct: this level of spending and external financing introduces significant balance sheet risk and potential shareholder dilution. The strategy hinges on generating a high return on this capital; if the payoff is delayed or smaller than hoped, the company will be left with a heavier debt load and a less flexible financial position.
A Squeeze On Profitability
This level of spending comes with an immediate and acknowledged cost to profitability. The business mix is shifting from high-margin software to what one analyst calls "capital-intensive AI infrastructure." articles.headline: What Could Go Wrong For Adobe Stock?
articles.text:
The company is deliberately sacrificing predictable profits for a long-term vision, but the timing of this high-stakes bet introduces its own unique risks.
If you're holding Adobe (ADBE) stock, you don't need me to tell you it's been a painful year. With the shares down almost fifty percent over the last twelve months, the market has clearly priced in a heavy dose of fear. The biggest risk now isn't some hidden threat, but whether the company's very public, very deliberate strategy to fix its problems creates even more of them.
Adobe is trading today's certainty for a bet on tomorrow, and it's doing so during a period of unusual vulnerability.
A Deliberate Trade-Off For Growth
The central issue is a major pivot in strategy. In response to competitive pressure and the rise of AI, management is aggressively pushing a "freemium" model for products like Firefly and Express. The goal is to attract hundreds of millions of new users. The cost, however, is immediate and clear. Management has explicitly stated this shift "lowers our second half ARR growth expectations."
This is more than a theoretical hit. The company has also decided to "defer previously planned Creative Cloud second half line optimizations," corporate-speak for shelving price hikes on its cash-cow products. The mechanism here is direct: the company is voluntarily giving up predictable, high-margin recurring revenue. This pressure (ARR) is the single most important metric for a subscription software business. While the company hopes this pays off with a larger user base to monetize later, management acknowledges the payback period is uncertain, suggesting it "will play out, I think, over 2027." That's a long time for investors to wait, especially when organic growth was already showing signs of strain, with one report noting "ten consecutive quarters of deceleration in revenue growth" after adjusting for a recent acquisition.

articles.headline: Oracle Is Burning Billions: Is IBM Stock The Smarter Cloud Play?
articles.text:
Oracle's (ORCL) stock is up by over 120% since the beginning of 2023. That is great for Oracle. But wait a minute, IBM's (IBM) stock is up a comparatively lower 91% during the same period. Hard to believe, but Oracle's stock appreciation is well ahead of IBM's stock. This is despite the stark contrast in how both companies generate cash. Over the trailing twelve months, IBM consistently generated massive free cash flow, pulling in a highly robust $12.2 billion. Oracle, over its most recently reported twelve-month period, recorded a staggering negative $23.7 billion in free cash flow as infrastructure spending wiped out its operating cash. Does that make sense? We do not think it does, and believe IBM presents a compelling valuation at current levels.
Image by JJ from Pixabay
The Cost Of Scaling: Oracle's CapEx vs. IBM's Free Cash Flow
Let us look at the core business prospects a bit more closely. Oracle has massive exposure to cloud services, bringing in $9.9 billion in total cloud revenue in its most recent quarter. Within this, its Cloud Infrastructure segment grew 93% to hit $5.8 billion. However, this growth requires monumental capital expenditures. To sustain this momentum, Oracle recently announced it expects to raise approximately $40 billion through a combination of debt and equity financing to fund its physical data center buildouts for AI workloads. This highly capital-intensive approach creates structural exposure for Oracle if broader enterprise spending on AI hardware infrastructure were to cool down, or if macroeconomic liquidity tightens, an outcome that could mirror shifts in digital asset markets where investors are weighing if Kevin Warsh will trigger a Bitcoin selloff.

articles.headline: Oracle Disputes Report on Failed Microsoft Cloud Deal
articles.text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Oracle (ORCL, Financials) pushed back against a report that said cloud deal talks with Microsoft had broken down.
Business Insider reported that Microsoft had explored leasing Oracle cloud infrastructure, but that talks fell apart over security and compliance concerns. The report said the deal could have been worth more than $3 billion.
Oracle said that version was not accurate.
The details mentioned in the article are inaccurate, an Oracle spokesperson said. The company also said Microsoft remains both a customer and a partner, and that the two sides continue to discuss ways to expand their work together.
Microsoft declined to comment. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report.
The dispute comes as cloud providers race to secure more capacity for artificial intelligence workloads. Microsoft has been investing heavily in Azure, while also looking for ways to manage demand from large customers.
For Oracle, the issue matters because its cloud business has become a bigger part of the company's growth story. Any sign of a strained relationship with Microsoft would draw investor attention, especially as both companies compete and cooperate in cloud infrastructure.

articles.headline: CoreWeave And The $40B Whisper
articles.text:
The AI infrastructure player popped on a technical benchmark, but the real story is the staggering size of the deals being signed behind the scenes.
It's not every day a stock surges +9.7% while the rest of the market takes a breather. But that's exactly what CoreWeave (CRWV) did on Tuesday, handily outperforming the broader technology sector as the S&P 500 slipped by -0.6%.
If you only read the press release, you'd think this was all about technical bragging rights.
More Than Just Speed
The company announced it had set new records in the MLPerf® Training v6.0 benchmark suite, a major benchmark for artificial intelligence hardware. CoreWeave's cloud infrastructure trained a massive model known as DeepSeek-V3 in a blistering 2.02 minutes. It's an impressive feat, a clear signal that its technology is at the bleeding edge of the AI arms race.
But that's not what had traders hitting the buy button.
A Whisper Louder Than A Press Release
While the engineers were celebrating, Wall Street was listening to a different story, courtesy of an analyst at Cantor Fitzgerald. The call was simple: investors are "Woefully Undervaluing" CoreWeave. The reason? The sheer scale of business the company is winning. According to the analyst, CoreWeave signed an incredible $40 billion in long-term contracts in the first quarter of this year. Even more startling was the suggestion that it "could sign another $40 billion in Q2."
Let's put that in perspective. This is a company with a market capitalization of about $61.7 billion. It's pulling in contracts that could soon eclipse its entire valuation, all while its revenue is already growing at 129.9% year over year. Of course, that growth comes at a cost; the company is still posting negative current operating margins of -2.6%.
The technology is clearly world-class, and the demand is immense. But with contracts this large piling up for a company still in the red, can management turn unprecedented demand into actual profit?
